n: The story pauses Joseph’s journey to follow Judah. Judah separates from his brothers and befriends a Canaanite man from Adullam, a town in the lowlands.

f.g: from Adullam, a town in the Judean foothills

n: Judah married a Canaanite woman, the very kind of marriage Abraham and Isaac had worked to avoid for their sons.

f.g: Strictly, Shuah is her father; she is called “the daughter of Shuah.”

n: Judah’s first son is born and named Er.
A second son, Onan, is born.
A third son, Shelah, is born at Chezib. Shelah’s descendants are listed later among the clans of Judah.
Judah arranged a marriage for his oldest son with a woman named Tamar, who becomes the central figure of this chapter.
Er’s specific sin is not described, but it was serious enough that the Lord took his life.

f.g: Printed in small capitals, this stands for the divine name YHWH (Jehovah).

n: Judah instructs Onan to follow an ancient custom: a brother should marry his brother’s widow so a child could carry on the dead man’s name and inheritance.

f.w: raise up seed to thy brother
f.g: the custom later called levirate marriage

n: Onan took the privileges of marriage but deliberately refused to give Tamar a child, because the heir would not count as his. He was cheating both his brother and Tamar.

f.w: the seed should not be his
f.g: the child would be legally his brother’s heir

n: The Lord was displeased with Onan’s selfish deceit and took his life as well.
Judah promised Tamar his youngest son but privately feared Shelah would die too, so he sent her home with no real intention of keeping his word.
Years passed. After his wife’s death and mourning, Judah went to the sheep-shearing festival at Timnath, a time of feasting.

f.g: Timnah, a town in the hill country of Judah

n: Tamar learns Judah is traveling nearby, and she sees a chance to secure the justice he has denied her.
Realizing Judah would never give her Shelah, Tamar removed her widow’s clothing, veiled herself, and waited by the road at Enaim (“an open place”).

f.g: Hebrew Enaim, possibly a place name meaning “two springs”

n: Judah assumed the veiled woman by the road was a prostitute and did not recognize her.
Judah propositioned her. Tamar negotiated carefully, steering toward something that would later prove who he was.
Judah offered a young goat as payment. Tamar asked for a guarantee until he sent it—note the goat again, echoing the goat used to deceive Jacob.
Tamar asked for Judah’s personal identifiers: his seal (used to sign documents), its cord, and his staff—the ancient equivalent of an ID card and signature.

f.g: a personal seal, often worn on a cord around the neck
probably the cord on which the seal hung

n: Tamar quietly returned home and put her widow’s clothing back on, now carrying Judah’s child.
Judah sent his friend with the goat to reclaim his pledge, but the woman could not be found.
Hirah asks for the “cult prostitute,” using a more respectable word, but the locals said there had been no such woman.

f.g: Here Hebrew qedeshah, a woman linked with pagan shrines, a different word than in verse 15.

n: Hirah reports back that the woman has vanished and no one knows of her.
Judah decides to drop the matter to avoid embarrassment, letting the woman keep his seal and staff.
When Tamar’s pregnancy became known, Judah—quick to judge others—ordered her executed for adultery, since she was promised to Shelah.
Tamar quietly sent Judah his own seal, cord, and staff: “Recognize these?” It is the same word his brothers used when they handed Jacob Joseph’s robe.
Judah confessed: “She is more righteous than I.” This is a turning point—Judah begins to take responsibility, preparing him to offer himself for Benjamin later.

f.w: She hath been more righteous than I

n: Tamar gives birth to twins, an echo of Rebekah’s twins, Esau and Jacob.
One twin put out a hand first, and the midwife tied a red thread to mark him as firstborn.
But the other brother pushed out first and was named Pharez (“breach” or “breaking through”). He became an ancestor of King David and of Jesus Christ.
Then the twin with the scarlet thread was born and named Zarah (“shining” or “dawn”). Once again in Genesis, the younger takes the place of the elder.
